summary: Defines a baseline way to encode Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) marks in IP packets and to carry that information across a Diffserv domain. PCN protects the quality of inelastic flows by marking packets when traffic goes above configured thresholds. It was replaced by RFC 6660.

plainLanguage.summary: A road can put up warning flags before it fills up. This document says how routers mark packets with those early warnings so important traffic like phone calls is protected. It was replaced by RFC 6660.

questions: how is pcn encoded in ip packets
subtitle: How routers mark packets with pre-congestion warnings using bits in the IP header.

tldr.problem: Networks need to protect quality of service for important traffic (like voice calls) from being degraded by overload. By the time traditional congestion is detected, it is too late to prevent quality loss.
tldr.mechanism: Pre-Congestion Notification marks packets early, before the network actually gets congested, giving admission-control systems a signal to reject new flows or terminate existing ones. This RFC specifies how to encode those marks in the IP header using the ECN field and a Diffserv codepoint.
tldr.outcome: The baseline encoding provides two states (marked and not marked) by redefining ECN codepoints. The scheme was later extended by RFC 6660 to provide more marking levels.

today: RFC 5696 was superseded by RFC 6660, which provides an updated PCN encoding scheme.

sections.title: Pre-Congestion Notification for QoS Protection
sections.content:
Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) is a way to protect quality of service for inelastic flows (like voice and video calls) within a network domain. Instead of waiting for actual congestion to occur, routers monitor traffic and mark packets when the rate exceeds certain configured thresholds—thresholds set below the link capacity.

These marks are then evaluated at network boundaries to decide whether to admit new flows or, in rare cases, terminate existing flows. Because the marking happens before congestion, the network can maintain QoS for admitted flows.

This RFC specifies the baseline encoding: how to mark packets in IP headers using the ECN field (normally used for end-to-end Explicit Congestion Notification). The baseline provides two PCN states: Not-marked (packets not yet marked) and PCN-marked (packets that have been marked).
sections.plainLanguage: Before a road gets crowded, it marks cars with a flag. Fewer new cars are let on until traffic clears. The flag uses a 2-bit field in the packet that normally means something else.

sections.title: Encoding Two PCN States in IP
sections.content:
The PCN encoding uses two parts of the IP header: the Diffserv codepoint (DSCP) and the ECN field (the last 2 bits of the IP ToS byte).

For a PCN-compatible DSCP, the four ECN codepoints are redefined:

  • 00 (not-ECT): not-PCN — packets not capable of PCN
  • 10 (ECT(0)): NM (Not-marked) — PCN-capable but not yet marked
  • 01 (ECT(1)): EXP — reserved for experimental schemes
  • 11 (CE): PM (PCN-marked) — marked by a PCN-interior-node

PCN-traffic MUST use a PCN-compatible DSCP. Non-PCN-traffic sharing the same DSCP MUST be marked as not-PCN (00). If traffic arrives with the ECN field already set to something other than not-ECT, the ingress node must handle it carefully to comply with RFC 3168 (ECN) semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: The encoding reuses a 2-bit field normally used for congestion signals. Each pattern means: unmarked, marked, not-PCN, or experimental.

sections.title: Marking and Transition Rules
sections.content:
At the PCN-ingress-node: All packets from a PCN-flow are marked with the Not-marked (10) codepoint. All other packets with the same DSCP are marked as not-PCN (00).

At PCN-interior-nodes: When metering algorithms determine that a packet should be marked, the PCN codepoint is set to 11 (PCN-marked). The following transitions are valid:

  • 10 (NM) → 11 (PM): marking a not-yet-marked packet
  • 01 (EXP) → 11 (PM): marking experimental traffic (to ease experimental scheme deployment)
  • 11 (PM) → 11 (PM): already marked, remains marked

Once a packet reaches 11, it can never change. All other transitions are invalid.

At PCN-egress-nodes: Packets leaving the domain should be reset to not-ECT (00), unless the egress node is certain that revealing other codepoints is safe (for example, if ECN-capability was explicitly negotiated).
sections.plainLanguage: A packet gets a flag when traffic is heavy. Once flagged, it stays flagged. New packets start unflagged, and old packets with experimental flags can be flagged too.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Design Rationale
sections.content:
The baseline encoding redefines the meaning of the ECN field only for PCN-compatible DSCPs. This allows the same DSCP to carry both PCN-traffic and non-PCN-traffic by marking non-PCN packets with 00. Non-PCN traffic is unaffected.

The choice of 10 for Not-marked (rather than 01) was made to ensure that PCN marks (11) survive tunneling through IP-in-IP or IPsec tunnels, since 11 is the only ECN codepoint guaranteed to be copied to outer headers. The encoding closely mirrors ECN semantics, which simplifies understanding and deployment.

When PCN domains are bounded by ingress and egress nodes that reset ECN fields, the scheme prevents unintended leakage of PCN marks into or out of the domain, maintaining backward compatibility with existing ECN implementations outside the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Non-flagged traffic is treated normally. Flagged traffic survives tunnels. When traffic leaves the PCN domain, the flags are cleaned off so outside networks don't see them.

sections.title: Deployment and Experimental Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC does not mandate a single DSCP for PCN because different operators may use different service classes (voice, video, conferencing) and have different network topologies. Instead, it provides guidance on suitable DSCPs drawn from admission-controlled classes such as Telephony (EF), Real-time Interactive (CS4), Broadcast Video (CS3), and Multimedia Conferencing (AF4).

The baseline encoding reserves the 01 codepoint for experimental use, with rules to ensure backward compatibility: all future schemes MUST treat 00 as not-PCN, MUST treat 11 as indicating PCN-marking, and MUST define all valid codepoint transitions. This allows new schemes to add finer granularity of marking while coexisting with baseline nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks can pick different DSCPs based on their traffic. Experimental schemes can add more flag patterns, but must follow rules so all routers understand the basics.
